cues.say: Component twenty-three: security basics.
Security basics are five habits you can name in one breath. HTTPS everywhere. Secrets in a vault. Let the payment provider handle cards. Least privilege. And keep little personal data.
In a design interview, that takes about twenty seconds. Then you go back to the design.
Why do they matter? Small shops get hurt by simple mistakes: a password left in the code, card numbers in their own database, or a worker that can read everything.
One attacker finds one hole, and everything behind it is exposed.
First, HTTPS everywhere. It encrypts traffic between the browser and your servers, so someone on the same cafÃ© Wi-Fi sees only noise.
Second, secrets in a vault. The Stripe key and the database password live in a secrets manager, not in the code. The API fetches them when it starts.
Third, hosted checkout. Customers type their card on Stripe's page, so card numbers never touch your servers. Stripe just tells you: order forty-two is paid.
Fourth, least privilege: each part gets only what it needs. The text worker can read the queue, but not the database.
Fifth, keep little personal data. A name and a phone number are enough. What you never store can't leak.
So in the interview, name these five, quickly and plainly.
And skip the deep cuts, like cipher suites and key lengths, unless you're asked.
Here's how it plays out. The interviewer asks: what about security?
The weak answer spends ten minutes on encryption algorithms, and there's no time left for go-live.
The strong answer names the five, with your design's details, in about twenty seconds.
Then you move on to go-live, with time to spare.
Here's where it sits: across the whole system. HTTPS at the front, keys from a vault, cards at Stripe, and narrow access for each part.
Two words to keep straight. Authentication is proving who you are, like a login.
Authorization is what you're allowed to do once you're in.
In the interview, say: HTTPS everywhere, secrets in a vault, no card data on our servers, and each service gets only what it needs.
